coredata.dc:description: Different delignification processes lead to significant differences in the structure and activity of lignin. Consequently, complex modifications are necessary before lignin to be applied. In this paper, a green process for the selective catalytic extraction of lignin by geopolymer is proposed based on biomass refining. This process can obtain lignin with ideal performance on activity, crosslink ability and curability. Taking eucalyptus, fir and bagasse as examples, the optimal lignin yields reach 46.5 %, 34.8 % and 48.7 % respectively (mFiber/mGeopolymer = 3, 120 min, and 130 °C). Moreover, lignin isolated with geopolymer (GL) shows a similar narrow molecular weight distribution range to that of Milled Wood Lignin (MWL). Studies on crosslinking solidification mechanisms have demonstrated that the phenolic hydroxyl groups of GL participate in the formation of a multi-stage amine crosslinking and solidification network structure. GL does not rely on flexible chains in the crosslinking and solidification of wood adhesives. Since highly active lignin can condense with phenolic hydroxyl groups on the surface of wood, it provides the adhesive with higher bonding strength (3.8 MPa). This study presents a novel approach to fabricating lignin-based formaldehyde-free wood adhesives.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: Different delignification processes lead to significant differences in the structure and activity of lignin. Consequently, complex modifications are necessary before lignin to be applied. In this paper, a green process for the selective catalytic extraction of lignin by geopolymer is proposed based on biomass refining. This process can obtain lignin with ideal performance on activity, crosslink ability and curability. Taking eucalyptus, fir and bagasse as examples, the optimal lignin yields reach 46.5 %, 34.8 % and 48.7 % respectively (mFiber/mGeopolymer = 3, 120 min, and 130 °C). Moreover, lignin isolated with geopolymer (GL) shows a similar narrow molecular weight distribution range to that of Milled Wood Lignin (MWL). Studies on crosslinking solidification mechanisms have demonstrated that the phenolic hydroxyl groups of GL participate in the formation of a multi-stage amine crosslinking and solidification network structure. GL does not rely on flexible chains in the crosslinking and solidification of wood adhesives. Since highly active lignin can condense with phenolic hydroxyl groups on the surface of wood, it provides the adhesive with higher bonding strength (3.8 MPa). This study presents a novel approach to fabricating lignin-based formaldehyde-free wood adhesives.

ce:section.ce:para: Lignin, a renewable aromatic natural polymer second only to cellulose, is an ideal substitute for non-renewable energy [1]. The intricate cross-linked structure of lignin binds cellulose and hemicellulose together, endowing the plant cell wall with strength and stiffness [2], yet simultaneously increasing the difficulty of biomass refining [3]. Currently, one of the largest sources of lignin is biorefinery, as well as the black liquor from the papermaking and pulping industry, with an annual output exceeding 50 million tons. The vast majority of these lignins (> 95 %) are utilized as fuel for heat recovery and power generation, while only approximately 2 % of industrial lignin is put to use [4]. Due to its abundant phenolic groups, excellent stiffness, high carbon content, biodegradability and thermal stability [5], lignin has been applied in elastomers [6], resins [7–9], adhesives [10], rubber [5], carbon materials [11], and other materials to enhance solidification performance. However, traditional alkali extraction of lignin is often accompanied by the fragmentation of lignin, resulting in significant heterogeneity and inhomogeneity. The direct introduction of this extracted lignin into the polymer system will give rise to issues such as poor dispersion, incompatibility, and instability [12]. To facilitate better application of lignin in various material fields, lignin modification is of great necessity. To date, various modification methods on lignin have been reported, including phenolation, esterification and solvent extraction [13,14]. Nevertheless, cumbersome steps and high costs limit its large-scale application.

Following the lignin priority separation and extraction strategy, accurately and effectively extracting lignin from biomass with high activity and low heterogeneity poses a significant challenge for enhancing its added value [15]. Researchers have proposed numerous processes for removing lignin to maintain the native structure and highly active groups of lignin [16]. In addition to the commercialized acid pretreatment and alkali pretreatment [17], other methods such as biological enzymes [18], organic solvents [19], and ionic liquids [20] have also been developed to extract highly active lignin. However, the above extraction processes have certain drawbacks, such as high cost and environmental pollution, making them non-compliant with the green extraction process of lignin [21]. Milled wood lignin (MWL) and enzymatic hydrolysis lignin (CEL), which are closer to the original lignin, can achieve minimal changes in the original structure of lignin due to the mild acid milling processes and cellulase enzymatic hydrolysis extraction process [22–24]. Moreover, MWL has drawn considerable attention in elucidating the structure of lignin and related reaction mechanisms because of its structure being closest to native lignin [25]. Nevertheless, the long and complex extraction process of MWL and CEL did not bring any increases in lignin yield, which greatly hampered its practical application [26]. Therefore, it is essential to find a green and efficient method for extracting proto-lignin that can not only achieve high lignin yield but also control the molecular weight range and uniformity of lignin products [4].

Can we find a extraction process that are more environmentally friendly, efficient, and closer to proto-lignin? Fortunately, our group discovered that alkaline geopolymers can selectively remove lignin from various biomass at low temperature (90 °C). This is a green process with recyclable lignin, low pollution, and no need to discharge wastewater [27]. Specifically, the lignin isolated with geopolymer (GL) owns high activity and capability of crosslink and solidify. It also has a large molecular weight and a narrow distribution range. Its structure is similar to that of MWL and is very similar to the original lignin. This specific molecular weight and uniformity of GL can serve as a macromolecular polymer skeleton or reinforcing material to enhance the mechanical properties of polymer composites. In this study, the process parameters of GL under different temperature conditions were further optimized based on previous work. In the meanwhile, the structural characteristics of GL represented by eucalyptus (hardwood), Fir (softwood), and bagasse (non-wood), as well as their corresponding MWL, were investigated. Finally, the obtained GL was directly combined with the curing agent to synthesize curable solidifiable resin and wood adhesives respectively, to explore the performance of this unmodified GL in direct crosslinking and solidification.

Eucalyptus chips, fir sawdust and bagasse, obtained from Ruizhou Industrial Co., Ltd. located in Shenzhen, China, were milled with a crusher and then sieved through a 60–80 mesh. The tree ages of eucalyptus and fir are 5 years and 10 years respectively. The resultant fibers were collected and dried in an oven at 80 °C. Metakaolin was procured from Super New Material Co., Ltd. in Inner Mongolia, China. The alkaline activator solutions with a desired modulus (Ms = nSiO2/nNa2O = 1.5 mol, solid content of 45.3 %) were prepared by mixing sodium hydroxide with sodium silicate solution (water glass) 24 h in advance to ensure complete dissolution and dissipation of the heat of hydration. The sodium silicate solution was obtained from Chunxu Chemical Co., Ltd. in Nanning, China. Solid sodium hydroxide tablets (96 % purity), sodium dodecyl sulphate (85 % purity), and 30 % hydrogen peroxide were supplied by Guanghua Sci-Tech Co., Ltd. in Guangdong, China. Deionized water was prepared in the laboratory. All the raw materials were utilized directly without any further purification.

Geopolymer was synthesized from metakaolin and prepared alkali activator solution. The alkali activator solution (100 g) was added to 100 g of metakaolin, and the mixture was stirred in a disperser at the speed of 1000 rpm for 3 min. Subsequently, 2 g of hydrogen peroxide and 0.2 g of sodium dodecyl benzene sulfonate were added and stirred at the speed of 1000 rpm for 1 min. The resulting slurry was injected into a plastic mold with dimensions of 100 × 50 × 30 mm3 and placed in an oven for curing at 60 °C. After being cured for 2 h, the sample was removed from the mold and subjected to further curing at 60 °C for 24 h. The main chemical component of the geopolymer is expressed by the oxide molar formula 0.45Na₂O·0.24Al₂O₃·SiO₂.

According to the work of Björkman [28], the MWLs of eucalyptus, fir and bagasse were prepared respectively. The biomass fibers were placed in a ball mill tank containing zirconia balls and ground at a speed of 400 rpm for 48 h. To prevent the temperature from exceeding its limits during the meticulous grinding process, the ball mill was suspended for a brief 10-min interval every 20 min. The biomass powder obtained through ball milling was immersed in a 1,4-dioxane/aqueous solution (96:4, v/v) at a solid-liquid ratio of 1:15 (g/mL). After stirring for 24 h, the mixture was centrifuged at a speed of 10,000 rpm. The separated solids were further washed with a 1,4-dioxane/aqueous solution (96:4, v/v) and centrifuged until the resulting supernatant was colorless and transparent. All the supernatants were evaporated and concentrated on a rotary evaporator, and the obtained concentrate was freeze-dried at −90 °C to obtain coarsely ground wood lignin. The crude MWLs were dissolved in an acetone/aqueous solution (9:1, v/v) and dropped dropwise into distilled water to precipitate lignin. The obtained lignin mixture was rotary evaporated at 50 °C to remove acetone and a large amount of water and then concentrated into a lignin suspension. After freeze-drying, the corresponding MWL was obtained.

GL were prepared based on our previous work [27]. The geopolymer pretreatment was carried out in a stainless-steel reactor (100 mL) with a polytetrafluoroethylene lining. Initially, 10 g of geopolymer, 30 g of biomass fiber (eucalyptus, fir, and bagasse), and deionized water (200 g) were heated to temperatures of 50, 70, 90, 110, 130, and 150 °C for durations of 30, 60, 90, 120, and 180 min respectively. After the pretreatment, the pre-treated biomass fibers were separated from the liquor by using a filter cloth and rinsed with deionized water. The resulting washing liquid and black liquor were collected together. Subsequently, a 50 % sulfuric acid solution was added to the black liquor until pH = 3. The precipitated lignin was separated and subjected to freeze-drying for 24 h to yield the GL powder.

Considering the low solubility of lignin, it is necessary to acetylate lignin to improve its solubility in DMSO [29]. The acetylation process of lignin was as follows [30]: 2.0 g of lignin was dissolved in 40 mL solution of pyridine: acetic anhydride (1:1, v/v) and stirred for 24 h at room temperature (25 °C). Then 15 mL of 1.5 % HCl was added at 0 °C, and the resulting precipitate was filtered and washed with deionized water to neutral. The acetylated lignin was finally dried for 24 h in the vacuum freezing machine.

2D-HSQC was used to determine the structure of lignin. 40 mg of acetylated lignin was dissolved in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO)-d6 (0.75 mL, containing 0.03 % Tetramethyl silane (TMS), v/v). 2D HSQC NMR (heteronuclear single-quantum coherence nuclear magnetic resonance) spectra were recorded on a Bruker AVANCE III 400 MHz spectrometer (Germany) at 400 MHz. The 2D HSQC NMR data were analyzed by MestraNova software and the DMSO central solvent peak was used as an internal reference (δC/δH = 39.5/2.49). The f1 (13C) and f2 (1H) frequency were 400.13 MHz and 100.62 MHz, respectively. The inter-scan relaxation delay was 2 s, and the spectral width was 24,148.754 Hz (F1) and 8012.820 Hz (F2). The number of composite points collected in the f2 dimension was 2048, the number of scans in the f1 dimension was 72, the 256-time increment and 145 Hz 1JCH were recorded.

Uncured adhesive samples were prepared by freeze-drying, while cured adhesive samples were sourced from hot-pressed plywood. The cured and uncured adhesives were analyzed using a Thermo Scientific K-alpha XPS spectrometer with Al Kα excitation (1486.6 eV), and the charge was corrected at the C 1 s binding energy of 284.8 eV.

Phenolic hydroxyl analysis was performed by UV–visible spectroscopy. As the phenolic hydroxyl group is deprotonated and red-shifted to phenolic ions in a strong alkaline solution, the concentration of the phenolic hydroxyl group can be determined by the adsorption difference between neutral and alkaline solutions [31]. Firstly, 5 mg of lignin sample was completely dissolved in 5 mL 0.2 N NaOH solution as a stock solution. Then, 0.12 mL of the stock solution was diluted to 3 mL with buffer solution (pH = 6, 0.05 M potassium dihydrogen phosphate and 0.006 M NaOH) as a neutral sample, and 0.2 N NaOH solution was used as an alkaline sample. The difference spectrum is determined by measuring the absorbance of the alkaline solution relative to the neutralized solution, and the neutralized solution is placed in an ultraviolet spectrophotometer as a blank to zero. The wavelength of 260 to 400 nm, the scanning speed of 1 nm/s, and the sum of the maximum values at 295 to 360 nm were selected as the non-conjugated phenolic structures. To prepare lignin-based resin, the dried unmodified lignin powders were mixed with deionized water to form a lignin concentrate with a solid content of 10 %. Polyamide (PA, molecular weight 650) was employed as the curing agent and 1,4-butanediol diglycidyl ether as the diluent. The above raw materials were stirred at a weight ratio of 10:0.1:1 to form a uniform slurry. The resultant slurry was poured into the polytetrafluoroethylene mold for the preparation of a dumbbell-shaped mold and then placed in a 60 °C vacuum drying oven to remove bubbles and continued to be maintained for 6 h to obtain a resin sample. The center width of the bio-resin material was 15 mm and the thickness was 1.0 mm, which was prepared in accordance with the GB/T 528–2009 standard. The tensile properties were measured and analyzed using a universal testing machine (WDW100) at a test rate of 1 mm/min.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Preparation of GL-based formaldehyde-free wood adhesives
ce:section.ce:para: The effect of lignin content on the bonding strength of plywood was studied through a one-way experiment. Polyamide (curing agent) is fixed at 10 % of the mass of 1,4-butanediol diglycidyl ether (crosslinking agent). Subsequently, the lignin is thoroughly mixed with the aforementioned curing and crosslinking agents. Samples with lignin addition levels of 50 %, 55 %, 60 %, 65 %, and 70 % are labeled as GL-50 %, GL-55 %, GL-60 %, GL-65 %, and GL-70 %, respectively. An appropriate amount of water is added to the mixture to adjust its solid content to 20 %. Then, stir the mixture for twenty minutes to ensure uniformity and finally obtain the lignin adhesive. The viscosity value of the adhesive is determined using a Brookfield DV-2 Pro viscometer. The final viscosity of each adhesive sample is measured three times and the numerical deviation is <100 mPa·s.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Preparation of three-layer plywood and evaluation of adhesive bonding performance
ce:section.ce:para: Three poplar veneers measuring 100 × 100 × 1.5 mm were used for three-layer plywood. The adhesive was evenly applied to one side of two veneers, with an application amount of 0.02–0.03 g/cm2 for each layer. The third veneer was sandwiched on the adhesive surface and placed on the heating plate of the hot press. Then, it was hot pressed at 2 MPa and 130 °C for 15 min to obtain a three-layer plywood sample. According to the national standard (GB/T 17657–2013), the bonding strength (both dry strength and wet strength) was measured and analyzed using a universal testing machine (WDW100) at a test rate of 2 mm/min. For the type II plywood wet strength test (GB/T 17657–2013), before the test, the specimens were pre-soaked in water at 60 ± 3 °C for 3 h and then dried at room temperature for 10 min.

In a controlled group experiment, MWL and alkaline lignin (AL) were used instead of GL to demonstrate the correlation between the number of phenolic hydroxyl groups and lignin activity. Furthermore, to demonstrate the potential application value of GL, lignin formaldehyde adhesive (LFA) was prepared by mixing lignin with formaldehyde (10 % based on lignin mass) for comparison. All the isolation experiments were performed at least three times to ensure reproducibility and avoid any experimental error.

The mechanism of formaldehyde-free wood adhesives was investigated by in-situ infrared spectroscopy (DRIFT). The spectra data were recorded using a Thermo Scientific Nicolet iS50 FT-IR Spectrometer (Massachusetts, America) equipped with an MCT detector cooled by liquid nitrogen (77 K) with KBr windows and an in-situ diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier transform spectroscopy accessory.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Efficiency and selectivity in extracting GL
ce:section.ce:para: To assess the efficiency of geopolymer pretreatment for lignin extraction, a process for extracting GL through geopolymer pretreatment was designed. The impacts of different reaction conditions on the delignification rate are presented in Fig. 1 . As illustrated in Fig. 1a, the lignin extraction rate declined with the increase in fiber mass ratio and geopolymer. Additionally, the lignin extraction rate of all fibers (eucalyptus, fir, and bagasse) also exhibited similar variations. However, further augmenting the geopolymer content when the fiber-to-geopolymer mass ratio exceeds 3 did not notably increase the lignin extraction yield. This might be due to the fact that the activation energy of the hydroxyl group is limited by temperature, making it difficult to destroy the dense structure inside the fiber and depolymerize the lignin deep within the fiber [27]. Consequently, mFiber/mGeopolymer = 3 is selected as one of the optimal parameters. As shown in Fig. 1b and c, the lignin yield of biomass fibers initially increased and then decreased with temperature. The optimum lignin extraction rates of eucalyptus, fir and bagasse at 130 °C for 120 min were 46.5 %, 34.8 %, and 48.7 %, respectively. High temperature disrupts the crystalline structure of lignocellulose and makes it loose, which is more conducive to the release of lignin [32]. Nevertheless, further heating will lead to lignin degradation, repolymerization, and a lower lignin extraction rate [32]. Among all fibers, fir had the lowest lignin extraction rate (34.8 %), which may be attributed to the fact that coniferous lignin typically contains more condensation bonds than hardwood lignin and is more difficult to depolymerize [33]. The high yield of bagasse lignin may be ascribed to the loose structure of grass, which is more favorable for the dissolution of lignin [34]. Fig. 1d shows the composition changes of fibers before and after the lignin extraction reaction. Almost no change in cellulose content was observed in all fibers, indicating that geopolymer pretreatment had minimal effect on cellulose during high-temperature delignification. For eucalyptus fibers, the lignin content decreased from 31.3 wt% to 18.5 wt% (~41 % lignin removal), while the cellulose and hemicellulose contents in the residue showed high retention rates of 99.5 % and 77.2 %, respectively. The lignin content of fir decreased from 26.4 wt% to 17.3 wt% (~34.5 % lignin removal), and the cellulose and hemicellulose contents in the residue retained 97.9 % and 71.1 %, respectively. The percentage content of cellulose and hemicellulose in bagasse retained 98.8 and 78.5 %, respectively, and the percentage content of lignin decreased from 22.7 % to 11.4 % (~50 % lignin removal). The above results demonstrate that the geopolymer can still achieve high selective delignification at high temperature (130 °C). Furthermore, a sustainable geopolymer pretreatment process was designed (Fig. 1e). After acidifying the black liquor produced by this process and filtering lignin precipitation, the filtrate adjusted to neutral can be recycled for at least 10 times. The COD, NH3-N, TSS, and lignin yield maintained a stable trend within a certain range with the reuse time of water (Fig. 1f). Hence, it is a green process for biomass refining based on geopolymer that involves the selective extraction of lignin without wastewater discharge.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Mechanism of GL extracted by geopolymer pretreatment
ce:section.ce:para: The changes in functional groups and lignin structure during delignification by extraction water were observed through the DRIFT (Fig. 2a-c). The DRIFT spectra at high temperature (130 °C) closely resemble those at low temperature (90 °C) in our previous study [27], and the infrared spectra of all fibers are significantly similar. The infrared absorption peaks at 1005 and 1002 cm−1 belong to the CO stretching mode of alcohol. The intensity of these peaks gradually shifts to 994, 975, and 960 cm−1 respectively, indicating the accumulation of trans olefin products [35]. Referring to the acknowledged mechanism of β-O-4 bond cleavage under high temperature alkaline reaction at elevated temperature [36], the possible cleavage mechanism of β-O-4 bond under high-temperature water-cooking condition is presented in Fig. 2d. The mechanism of delignification is similar to that of the traditional alkali method. Under the induction of the nucleophile (OH-) continuously provided by geopolymer, the α-alkoxides generated in the lignin macromolecules attack the vicinal β‑carbon atoms, and make OH- and carbon atoms connected to form an epoxy structure (compound I). The electron cloud of the oxygen atom on the hydroxyl group is shifted to the carbon atom, thereby weakening the interaction between the C and O atoms in the methoxy group, so that it is removed from the benzene ring, and finally new phenolic subunit and phenolic hydroxyl group are formed [37]. In the above process, 2-methoxyphenol (guaiacol) and α, β-epoxide intermediate (compound II) are generated with the cleavage of the β-O-4 bond. The nucleophilic reagent hydroxide ion attacks α‑carbon through nucleophilic addition reaction, opens the epoxy structure of compound I and converts it to 1-phenylglycerol (compound II). Then, the hydroxyl group on the β carbon of glycerol side chain is induced by geopolymer and forms protonated compound III. Due to the increase of negative charge of protonated hydroxyl, compound IV with trans olefin side is finally produced by dehydration [38–40].

ce:section.ce:section-title: The structural characteristics of MWL and GL
ce:section.ce:para: To elucidate the structure of MWL and GL, FT-IR spectra were recorded and presented in Fig. 3 . It was evident that the infrared spectra of MWL and the corresponding GL were highly similar. The absorption peaks at 3450 and 3420 cm−1 in Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy are attributed to the stretching vibration of OH. Higher infrared peaks indicate that GL has more hydroxyl functional groups compared to MWL. The absorption peaks at 2920 and 2850 cm−1 are attributed to the CH stretching vibrations of methyl and methylene, respectively. The stretching vibrations of the non-conjugated CO ester bond peak at 1750 cm−1 and the CO bond at 1233 cm−1 almost disappeared in GL, indicating that the lignin-carbohydrate ester was effectively cleaved by the geopolymer [41]. Peaks at 1600, 1510, and 1420 cm−1 were assigned to the aromatic-ring vibrations of lignin [42]. A peak at 1330 cm−1 was assigned to the CO of the syringyl (S) ring, and aromatic-ring vibrations at 1262 and 1123 cm−1 were attributed to guaiacyl (G) and S units, respectively. A band at 1048 and 1033 cm−1 was attributed to aromatic CH in-plane deformations (G > S), CO deformations, and CH stretching (non-conjugated) in primary alcohols, respectively [43]. Significantly, the infrared peak that disappears at 1010 cm−1 may be due to the breakdown of the hydroxyl OH bond in the unstable enol structure to form aldehydes or ketones [27].

The structural characteristics of MWL and GL were studied by 2D-HSQC NMR and assigned according to the previously published literature (Fig. 4 ) [26,44]. Since the aromatic ring unit of lignin remains relatively unchanged during the pretreatment process [45], the structure of lignin can be determined based on changes in the main bond connections in lignin (Table 1 ). The MWL spectra and S/G ratios of all fibers are very similar to those of GL. A high level of phenolic hydroxyl groups (up to 2.68 mmol/g) was detected, indicating that GL has higher activity than MWL. The correlation of S, G and H lignin units can be observed in the aromatic region of eucalyptus, fir and bagasse lignin, while only G and S lignin units were observed in the aromatic region of fir, which is consistent with the reported work literature [46]. The S lignin unit showed a significant signal of C2,6 -H2,6 correlation at δC/δ H 102.5–105.2/6.3–6.8, while the signal corresponding to C2,6 -H2,6 correlation in oxidized (C α = O) phenolic syringyl units (S′) was observed at δC/δ H 106.0/7. 4. The corresponding signals at δC/δ H 110.4–112.5/6.8–7.4, 114.8–120.8/6.7–7.2 and 124.4–130/6.8–7.4 were indicative of the presence of C2 -H2, C5 -H5 and C2,6 -H2,6 in guaiacyl units (G), respectively. In the signal of H lignin units corresponding to C2,6 -H2,6 in p − hydroxyphenyl (H) was showed at δC/δ H 124.9–125.8/7.32. In the side chain region (δC/δ H 50–90/2.5–6.5) of GL, the spectrum shows a significant signal corresponding to the β-O-4′ ether unit (A), where the signals at δC/δ H 77.8–82.5/4.5–5.0, 72.5–77.5/5.8–6.3 and 62.0–65.0/3.5–4.5 are attributed to C β -H β (S), C α -H α (G) and C γ -H γ of the β-O-4′ substructure (A), respectively.

The above results of 2D-HSQC NMR showed that the β-O-4′ structures in GL was effectively retained in the delignification process of geopolymer. The resin alcohol structure (B) present in the lignin side chain suggests that the ether bond in the side chain structure of GL is less depolymerized under the action of the nucleophile OH−, and the molecular structure of GL is complete.

The molecular weight distributions of GL and MWL were analyzed and characterized by gel permeation chromatography (GPC) as depicted in Fig. 5 . The GL of eucalyptus (Mw = 13,719, DPI = 1.4) has a larger molecular weight and a narrower dispersion compared to MWL (Mw = 8091, DPI = 2.2). The large molecular weight of GL implies that intact lignin molecules were successfully removed from the wood fibers by geopolymer pretreatment, which is in accordance with the results from the HSQC spectrum. However, for fir, the GL (Mw = 6306, DPI = 1.4) and MWL (Mw = 10,669, DPI = 1.4) exhibited an opposite pattern. This might be due to the low degree of delignification of coniferous wood (Fig. 1), and the low concentration of lignin in the solution is difficult to condense. For bagasse, there is no significantly difference in the molecular weights of the two kind of lignin, and the dispersion of GL was lower than that of MWL (1.7 versus 2.2). In conclusion, the peak shape of GL is more uniform than that of MWL, which is more conducive to the fractionation and high value-added utilization of lignin.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Crosslinking and solidification properties of GL
ce:section.ce:para: To evaluate the crosslinking and solidification properties of GL, GL-based resin and GL-based formaldehyde-free wood adhesive prepared from GL (eucalyptus) were shown in Fig. 6a and b, respectively. Although the resin was successfully cross-linked and cured by GL, its tensile strength and Young's modulus were only 2.0 MPa and 0.32 GPa, respectively (Fig. 6a). This result seems rather obvious. Due to the lack of suitable flexible chains such as epoxy resin, phenolic resin, etc., crosslinking and solidification based solely on rigid lignin cannot provide better mechanical properties for the resin [47]. On the other hand, a surprising result is that GL appears to have more advantages in wood adhesive applications. DSC analysis was used to study the curing behavior of GL resin and determine the hot-pressing temperature of plywood (Fig. 6c). Compared to GL, GLA has a slightly higher curing temperature. Based on the DSC analysis results, a hot-pressing temperature of 130 °C has been chosen. As shown in Fig. 6d, as the lignin content increases, the dry strength and wet strength of plywood first increase and then decrease. The loss of mechanical strength may be due to the low crosslinking density caused by excessive lignin [46]. At the same time, the viscosity of the adhesive gradually increased from 7.44 to 22.50 mPa·S. When the lignin content is 55 %, the dry strength and wet strength of plywood can reach up to 3.8 MPa and 2.4 MPa, respectively. The dry and wet strength of all adhesive boards are higher than 0.7 MPa, the required by the national standard (GB/T 17657–2013). The above results indicate that the crosslinking and curing of GL in adhesives do not seem to depend on flexible chains. Fig. 6e displays the molecular weights and phenolic hydroxyl groups of MWL, GL, and AL of eucalyptus wood, respectively. Compared to AL (4296 g/mol) and MWL (8091 g/mol), GL has the highest molecular weight (13,719 g/mol), and the number of phenolic hydroxyl groups in GL (2.45 mmol/g) is similar to that in AL (2.54 mmol/g). To clarify the relationship between phenolic hydroxyl groups and lignin activity, the bonding strength of plywood made from the above lignin was compared. As shown in Fig. 6f, the MWL with the lowest number of phenolic hydroxyl groups (1.32 mmol/g) has the lowest average dry strength (1.86 MPa) and wet strength (1.15 MPa). Although GL and AL have almost the same number of phenolic hydroxyl groups, the average dry strength (3.1 MPa vs 2.42 MPa) and wet strength (1.78 MPa vs 1.42 MPa) of GL are higher than those of AL. The above results indicate that the content of phenolic hydroxyl groups determines the activity of lignin. Meanwhile, lignin with higher molecular weight and better molecular uniformity helps improve the mechanical properties of lignin polymers [11]. Furthermore, due to the absence of necessary crosslinking agents and curing agents, pure lignin adhesives (GL) lack resistance to the deterioration effect caused by moisture [49]. This study also supplemented the bonding strength testing of plywood made of lignin phenolic resin. However, its water resistance cannot meet the requirements, which may be due to insufficient condensation reaction caused by insufficient formaldehyde [49]. Fig. 6g illustrates the scale-up test process for the formaldehyde-free adhesive, showcasing its potential for scale-up production.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Crosslinking and solidification mechanisms of GL
ce:section.ce:para: The crosslinking and solidification mechanism of unmodified GL in resin and adhesive systems was investigated using DRIFTS (Fig. 7a and b). The mechanism diagram of the resin and adhesive is presented in Fig. 7a. The original infrared spectra of resin and adhesive exhibited similar peaks. The intensity of the epoxy functional group's infrared peak was gradually reduced to 920 cm-1, and the tertiary amine peak at 1342 cm−1 was enhanced, which was attributed to the two-step addition reaction of 1,4-butanediol glycidyl ether and polyamide [48]. The branched chain characteristics of the multi-level amine are the key to constructing the lignin crosslinking condensation network. Unlike resin, as shown in Fig. 7b, the high-intensity infrared peak at 1138 cm−1 corresponds to the stretching of CO, which is caused by the ether bond and ester bond formed during the condensation of the adhesive and wood veneers. At the same time, the aromatic ring on the lignin is connected to the ester bond (p-π conjugation), which makes the bending vibration peak of the carbonyl group shift from 1074 to 1066 cm−1. The above characteristic peaks indicate that the hydroxyl groups on the wood play a role in the crosslinking and solidification of the adhesive, which also contributes to the high bonding strength of the adhesive (Fig. 7j-k).

To further illustrate the crosslinking and solidification mechanism of GL, XPS analysis was performed on uncured and cured adhesives (Fig. 7c-i). The corresponding elemental composition is shown in Fig. 7c. After the cure reaction, the C 1 s content decreased from 77.85 % to 75.73 %, while the N 1 s content increased from 16.64 % to 18.45 %, and the O 1 s content rose from 5.51 % to 5.82 %. The slight changes in composition may be attributed to the loss of volatile substances during hot pressing. In the XPS spectrum of the uncured adhesive, the C1 s nuclear level spectrum was fitted into three different peaks, which were the CC peak at 284.80 eV, the CO peak at 286.40 eV, and the O-C-O peak of the epoxy functional group at 288.22 eV (Fig. 7d). The N 1 s core level spectrum was fitted to two distinct peaks, 399.71 eV and 400.78 eV, corresponding to the CN and the NH peaks (Fig. 7e). The O 1 s core level spectrum was fitted to three peaks, namely the CO peak at 530.88 eV, the CO peak of the alcoholic hydroxyl group at 531.38 eV, and the CO peak of the phenolic hydroxyl group at 532.77 eV (Fig. 7f). In the XPS spectrum of the cured adhesive, three different peaks for the C 1 s curves appear at binding energies of 284.80, 286.28, and 288.00 eV, ascribed to the CC, CO, and O-C-O (Fig. 7g). Meanwhile, two different peaks at 399.9 (CN) and 401.73 (NH) are observed for N 1 s curves (Fig. 7h). The curve of O 1 s (Fig. 7i) exhibits three different peaks at 530.86 (C=O), 531.81 (CO), and 532.61 eV (COOR). The increase in CC bond content indicates that the cross-linking curing reaction occurred in the adhesive. The content of CN increased and NH bonds decreased significantly, which was consistent with the results of the synthesis of tertiary amines by polyamide in-situ infrared spectroscopy. Furthermore, the ester group at 532.61 eV shows that the phenolic hydroxyl group in lignin is involved in the esterification reaction [50]. It is worth mentioning that the entire adhesive application process does not involve the participation of aldehydes, indicating its potential to produce formaldehyde-free adhesives.

This paper proposes a green process for high-selective large-scale extraction of GL from geopolymers under high temperature conditions. The 2D-HSQC spectrum results showed that the GL in eucalyptus (hardwood), fir (softwood), and bagasse (non-wood) was very similar to its corresponding MWL. The high activity and cross-linking curing ability of GL were confirmed through the synthesis of lignin resin and adhesive. The multi-level amine structure formed by reacting phenolic hydroxyl groups of lignin with epoxy functional groups and amino groups forms a crosslinking and solidification network. The crosslinking and solidification of GL in adhesives does not depend on flexible chains. The condensation of the adhesive with the hydroxyl groups on the wood enhances its bonding strength (3.8 MPa). This study provides an effective method for the production and direct utilization of lignin, and confirms the enormous potential of GL as a wood adhesive.
